title: Air Courier Conference of America v. American Postal Workers Union (1991)
shortTitle: Air Courier Conference v. American Postal Workers Union
summary: Postal workers are outside the zone of interests of the Private Express Statutes, which protect Postal Service revenue rather than postal employment, so their unions could not challenge a suspension of the postal monopoly.
notes:
Key line: "The postal monopoly, therefore, exists to ensure that postal services will be provided to the citizenry at large, and not to secure employment for postal workers." Chief Justice Rehnquist, for the Court.

Citation: 498 U.S. 517 (1991).

sections.Parties: Petitioner was the Air Courier Conference of America, a trade association of private courier companies that benefited from the suspension of the postal monopoly. The United States Postal Service, a respondent under the Court's rules, supported the petitioner. Respondents were the American Postal Workers Union and other unions representing Postal Service employees. The unions argued that opening international mail to private couriers would cost postal workers jobs and that they were within the zone of interests protected by the statutes creating the postal monopoly.
sections.Material Facts: The Private Express Statutes, codified at 18 U.S.C. 1693 to 1699 and 39 U.S.C. 601 to 606, give the Postal Service a monopoly over the carriage of letters and were created as a revenue protection measure so the Service could fulfill its mission of universal service at uniform rates. Section 601(b) permits the Service to suspend the restrictions on any mail route where the public interest requires it. Using that power, the Postal Service issued a regulation authorizing international remailing, a practice in which private couriers carry letters destined for foreign addresses out of the country and deposit them with foreign postal services. The unions claimed that the rulemaking record did not support a finding that suspension served the public interest. The Postal Reorganization Act of 1970 reenacted the Private Express Statutes and separately added labor-management provisions to improve pay and working conditions for postal employees.
sections.Procedural History: The unions sued in the District Court for the District of Columbia under the APA. The District Court granted summary judgment to the Postal Service and the courier association. The D.C. Circuit vacated, holding that the unions satisfied the zone-of-interests test under Clarke v. Securities Industry Association and, on the merits, that the suspension was not justified by the public interest. The Supreme Court granted certiorari, heard argument on November 28, 1990, and reversed on February 26, 1991.
sections.Issue: Under the APA a plaintiff may obtain review only if the interest it asserts is arguably within the zone of interests protected or regulated by the statute it invokes. The unions claimed that suspending the postal monopoly for international remailing would divert mail to private couriers and cost postal workers jobs, and they pointed both to the Private Express Statutes and to the labor provisions of the Postal Reorganization Act. Are the employment interests of postal workers within the zone of interests protected by the Private Express Statutes, so that their unions may obtain APA review of the Postal Service's suspension decision?
sections.Holding: No. The language and legislative history of the Private Express Statutes show that Congress created the postal monopoly to protect Postal Service revenues and enable universal service, not to protect postal employment. The labor-management provisions of the Postal Reorganization Act have no integral relationship with the monopoly provisions and cannot be used to bring the unions within the zone. Because the unions lacked standing, the Court did not reach the merits. The judgment was reversed.
sections.Reasoning: Chief Justice Rehnquist first declined to decide whether 39 U.S.C. 410(a) exempts the Postal Service from APA review, because the question had not been raised below. Turning to standing, he explained that the zone-of-interests test asks whether the plaintiff's interest is arguably within the zone of interests protected or regulated by the statutory provision at issue. The monopoly dates from the Articles of Confederation and has always been justified as a means of securing revenue so the Service can provide service to all communities at a uniform rate by preventing private couriers from skimming profitable routes. The statutory text confirms that focus, and nothing in the legislative history suggests concern with postal jobs. The unions argued that Clarke permitted courts to consider related provisions, and they pointed to the labor-management sections of the Postal Reorganization Act. The Court distinguished Clarke, where the provisions at issue were parts of an integrated statutory scheme addressing the same subject. The labor provisions and the monopoly provisions have no integral relationship, and the legislative history reveals no connection. Saying that the monopoly is the linchpin of the Service and that the labor provisions benefit workers stretches the test too far, because it would let any beneficiary of any part of a large statute challenge any violation of any other part.

topics.lrs-n-standing-zone: NCUA debates how this limiting example fits its more generous competitor analysis.
topics.lrs-n-standing-apa702: The unions sued under the APA's judicial-review provisions, and the Court framed the zone-of-interests inquiry as a limit on who is 'aggrieved' under § 702.
topics.lrs-k-statutory-structure: The holding turns on refusing to read the Private Express Statutes together with the Postal Reorganization Act's separate labor-management provisions when identifying the relevant statute.

learning.separateOpinions: The judgment was unanimous. Justice Stevens concurred in the judgment, joined by Justices Marshall and Blackmun, reasoning that 39 U.S.C. 410(a) unambiguously exempts the Postal Service from the APA's judicial review provisions, so the unions had no cause of action regardless of the zone-of-interests analysis.
